assessment.nobel_worthiness: A new observational window: IceCube turned a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice into a neutrino telescope and established a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos (2013), later supported by evidence for TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane. As an instrument-driven astroparticle result it is original, clear and likely to last.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led IceCube and AMANDA and drove the science case; Spiering was a long-standing leader of the detector's development and the neutrino-astronomy programme in the DESY/Baikal/AMANDA/IceCube lineage. Two names fit the supplied credit, though the contribution of the wider collaboration and earlier DUMAND/Baikal pioneers is not captured.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is confirmed in several channels and independently by ANTARES/KM3NeT-type data. Sources are only partly identified, but the detection itself is robust and the field is established.
uncertainties: Individual attribution within a large collaboration and the roles of earlier pioneers (DUMAND, Baikal) are not fully resolved.
The identity of most neutrino sources remains open, so the astrophysical interpretation is still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental observation of the Higgs boson at the LHC completed the Standard Model and was a landmark in detector technology and in the physics of the electroweak sector. Its importance and clarity are beyond doubt; the theory half was recognised in 2013.
assessment.attribution: The names supplied are founders/leaders of ATLAS and CMS, which is a defensible but unavoidably partial way to credit thousands of collaborators and the accelerator builders. Whether the committee can find a fair, rule-compliant configuration is the central problem.
assessment.maturity: Mature: independently observed by two experiments, with couplings measured to growing precision through Run 2 and Run 3.
uncertainties: Attribution to individuals for a collaboration discovery is the main obstacle; spokespersons are not necessarily the decisive contributors.
Statutes limit recipients to three and the 2013 prize already recognised the theory, so the committee may judge experimental recognition differently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of the double pulsar PSR J0737-3039A/B gave a uniquely clean strong-field laboratory: multiple independent post-Keplerian tests of general relativity, including the Shapiro delay and the spin-orbit effect, with sub-0.1 percent precision. Timing methodology and long-term calibration are the real strengths.
assessment.attribution: Burgay found the system in the Parkes multibeam survey, Lyne led the team and the discovery of the B pulsar, and Kramer led the long-term timing and the GR tests. The credit seems separable and fair for three people.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by years of timing at several observatories, with results stable and improved over time. Timely, and complements the 1993 Hulse-Taylor prize and the 2017 gravitational-wave prize.
uncertainties: Hulse-Taylor already recognised binary pulsar tests of GR, so the committee may see this as incremental in principle.
Burgay's junior role at discovery versus the timing leaders could be debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, reached 10^-18 fractional uncertainty and underpin a redefinition of the second, tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. This is precision measurement at its best: new technique, deep systematics control, and a wide range of applications.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated Sr clocks; Ye developed the very high stability and accuracy and the comparison with frequency combs. Two names are a clean and widely accepted pairing, and the frequency comb prize (2005) is a separate piece.
assessment.maturity: Mature: many independent clocks (Sr, Yb, Hg) agree at the 10^-18 level and national metrology institutes are moving towards a redefinition. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: This is outside my own expertise, which I take from colleagues; the relative weight of Katori, Ye and others such as Hall and Hänsch's earlier prize is something I cannot judge independently.
Whether the committee sees a clock as a discovery or as technology could affect support.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping and cooling antihydrogen and measuring it precisely (ALPHA spectroscopy, gravitational behaviour; BASE antiproton magnetic moment and charge-to-mass ratio) tests CPT symmetry and the matter-antimatter asymmetry with extreme precision. It is close to my own field of antimatter, and I value the experimental craft involved.
assessment.attribution: Gabrielse pioneered antiproton and positron trapping (and the ATRAP effort), Hangst leads ALPHA, Ulmer leads BASE. The three-name split follows distinct experimental approaches, although ATRAP and ASACUSA/AEgIS contributions are also relevant.
assessment.maturity: Results are confirmed by independent traps and groups, though most findings are consistency tests that find no violation. This is mature as technique, but the physics outcome is a null result.
uncertainties: Null results for CPT and weak equivalence may weigh less than a positive discovery.
Competition between ALPHA and ATRAP means credit for first trapping and spectroscopy could be disputed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first horizon-scale images of the shadow of M87* and then Sgr A* are a strong, communicable observational achievement, with global VLBI at 1.3 mm as the novel instrument. It directly tests strong-field gravity and black-hole physics.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept, Doeleman led the EHT instrument and collaboration, Zensus led the European/MPIfR side and the mm-VLBI development. A fair configuration is possible but the 300-strong collaboration makes it contested.
assessment.maturity: Recent (2019, 2022), but the images have been reproduced by independent reductions and further epochs. The scientific interpretation, e.g. spin and jet launching, is still evolving, so it may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Collaboration-scale credit and the roles of Bouman and others who developed imaging algorithms are not captured by the list.
Interpretation is model-dependent in parts; recognition may be premature relative to the longer-term follow-up.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of X-ray, optical and radio afterglows of gamma-ray bursts, enabled by the BeppoSAX wide-field cameras, settled the cosmological origin of GRBs and opened an entire branch of high-energy astrophysics. A clear case of an instrument creating a discovery.
assessment.attribution: Costa and Frontera led the BeppoSAX GRB monitor and narrow-field follow-up that gave arcminute positions; Kulkarni's team obtained the optical/radio counterparts and redshift. Credit is reasonably separable, but van Paradijs and Groot and others also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Mature: nearly 30 years of confirmation by Swift, Fermi and gravitational-wave coincidence (GW170817), with the cosmological origin undisputed.
uncertainties: Other key people such as van Paradijs (deceased) and the optical groups limit a clean three-person split.
The Nobel committee has not recently favoured high-energy astrophysics, so timing is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Silicon microstrip and hybrid/3D pixel detectors made precise vertexing and tracking possible at high rates, underpinning heavy-flavour physics, the Higgs and top measurements at the LHC and later imaging applications. Enabling instrumentation of this kind is exactly what I know best, and the lasting impact is large.
assessment.attribution: Parker developed 3D and microstrip silicon concepts, Heijne pioneered silicon pixel/hybrid readout, and Campbell led the Medipix/hybrid pixel work. The credit is plausible but other pioneers (e.g. Hyams, Kemmer, Rancoita, Lutz) and the large LHC detector teams also contributed, so the allocation is not obviously complete.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature: silicon trackers have run for decades in many experiments with independent implementations and continued evolution.
uncertainties: Whether a detector-technology prize fits the Nobel physics criteria in the committee's view, given past instrumentation prizes such as Charpak's in 1992.
Attribution among several overlapping silicon-detector inventors is only partly resolved by the supplied credit.
